extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature; literary critics analyzing representation of the supernatural and allegory (e.g., Bunyan, Milton)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging how the supernatural, divine subjects, and allegory are represented in poetry and prose, with examples drawn from Milton and John Bunyan; focuses on suitability of subject, authorial stance, characterization, and techniques for plausibility. Useful for critics or students assessing religious/phantasmatic literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial belief in the supernatural
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist must himself believe in the supernatural, or his description of it will be a sham, without dignity and without credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual support: 'The artist must himself believe in the supernatural, or his description of it will be a sham, without dignity and without credibility.' Example: Benvenuto Cellini's vision enabled a convincing image of the Virgin. Anti-pattern: a writer treating apparitions as mere literary devices without inner conviction produces hollow representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of imagination (not servile literalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist must be 'able at the same time to treat the subject which he selects with freedom, throwing his own mind boldly into it,' otherwise he will produce 'the hard and stiff forms of literal tradition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: do not be a servile copyist of reported visions or traditions; transform and re-shape the material imaginatively. Example contrast: Cellini uses vision but also his own mind; a merely literal treatment results in stiffness and lack of dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epochal/cultural condition for successful supernatural art
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful representation of the supernatural depends on a particular historical/mental condition — a twilight of belief when imagination can re-shape religious tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The condition is 'extremely peculiar' and 'necessarily transitory.' Critics should evaluate whether the cultural context allows audience imaginative assent; outside such an epoch, portrayals may either offend believers or ring false to sceptics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attempting what the author cannot comprehend
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must himself comprehend the character he creates 'to its inmost fibre'; he cannot create a character he cannot comprehend (and cannot comprehend his own Creator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the author lacks inward understanding of a being (especially the Infinite), attempts to present it as a full personality will fail. Anti-pattern: giving God or the Absolute ordinary human psychology because the poet cannot genuinely grasp the divine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect limits when representing the Infinite/God
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should not make the unlimited and incomprehensible Being 'talk like an ordinary man' or 'describe his feelings and his purposes'; such anthropomorphism is a 'trespass beyond the permitted limits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply negative theology or restraint: speak of the Infinite by negatives or leave much unstated. Example of failure: Milton's Councils of the Trinity 'talking like Puritan divines' which provokes incredulity in the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-to-genre suitability (scale and ambition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grand theological or supernatural subjects may be unsuited to certain literary treatments; whether a subject is handled as literal fact or as legend/myth determines appropriate artistic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Paradise Lost' is caught between treating its subject as literal history and as myth, producing a sense of unsatisfactoriness. Guideline: match ambition of form (poem vs prose; attempt at sublimity) to how the subject can be imaginatively handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive detailed elaboration on incomprehensible themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Fullness of detail on a theme 'so far beyond our understanding is as dangerous as vague grandiloquence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tackling transcendent topics, restraint is required — too much minute detail can produce discord and lessen credibility. Example: 'The Holy War' suffers from 'fulness of detail' that endangers the work's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegorical personifications must be substantively humanized
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical characters (virtues/vices) succeed only when 'substantiated into persons' — i.e., made into representative realities with recognizable human traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive example: characters in 'Pilgrim's Progress' (Mr. Pliable, Mr. Obstinate, etc.) are 'representative realities' that 'bleed' and 'laugh.' Anti-pattern: allegory that remains merely abstract and fails to evoke human sympathy or recognition, as in parts of 'The Holy War.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of incidental, irrelevant particulars to create realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Little touches and needless particulars irrelevant to the general plot (e.g. 'I do not know,' 'He did not tell me this') create the illusion of reality and give a work the air of reportage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique guidance: include small, seemingly irrelevant details and digressions to make fiction feel authentic. Example: Bunyan's manner like Defoe's — the introduction of life-like minutiae makes readers believe they are reading real history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer naturalistic machinery over melodramatic retribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not spoil a natural story with melodramatic, sensational judgments; natural, believable consequences are often more artistically effective than artificial poetic retribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bunyan's choice: he avoids abrupt sensational punishment and instead lets 'natural machinery' and plausible consequences (ill-health, ruin, domestic retribution) carry moral weight. Anti-pattern: contriving miraculous or overwrought punishments solely to moralize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance making a villain interesting with theological fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a villain (e.g., Satan) interesting, the writer may need to add noble touches, but doing so risks transforming him away from the traditional theological figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical tension: assess whether added nobility or complexity enhances literary interest at the cost of doctrinal fidelity. Example: making Satan 'interesting' may make him a 'nobler' figure and thereby cease to be the Satan of Christian religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align treatment with audience belief and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's treatment must consider whether the audience regards the subject as literal fact or as legend; when belief is 'consciously gone' the poet lacks reverence and cannot inspire; when belief is too complete the poet dares not innovate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the intended audience's stance toward religious truth affects the plausibility and reception of supernatural representation. Anti-patterns: treating sacred history as playground when believers expect literal truth; or refusing imaginative treatment when audience views subject as myth.
